sections.heading: Before the Therefore
pulls: The Good News is not good advice for the dust-man. It is the news that he has already been declared righteous in Christ.
paras: Romans 6 opens with a question: “What shall we say then?” A question like that reaches back over everything Paul has already said, and you cannot answer it until you have heard the setup. So before you walk into chapter 6, stand where the first five chapters put you. It is hard ground. Guilty as dust. Then, from nowhere you could earn, declared righteous. Condemned, then acquitted. An enemy of God, then at peace with Him. Skip that, and the rest of the letter floats. This first week lays the foundation the whole study stands on: the Good News underneath the walk.

This matters for a man in the dust. You probably fight sin from the wrong side of the verdict, as though this week’s behavior decides whether God is for you. Paul turns that around. He does not say, clean yourself up and you may find peace with God. He says the peace is already made and the verdict already spoken, and on that settled ground you learn to live. Revival never starts with what you do for God. It starts with what God has already done for you in Christ.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: The Diagnosis: All Under Sin
paras: Paul spends nearly three chapters taking away every place to hide. The openly pagan are without excuse (Romans 1). The morally respectable are without excuse (Romans 2). The religious insider is without excuse (Romans 3). Then comes the verdict that levels the room: “There is no one righteous; no, not one” — “for all have sinned, and fall short of the glory of God.” This is the dust at its most honest. Not that you are as bad as you could be, but that no corner of you is untouched, and no ladder reaches high enough to climb out.

You resist this, because you grade yourself on a curve against other men. But the curve is not the standard. The glory of God is. Measured there, the strong and the weak, the decent and the scandalous, all land in the same place: short. This is not cruelty. It is a doctor who will not lie to a dying patient, because a disease you will not name is a disease you cannot treat. The dust has to be told the truth before it can be revived.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: The Verdict Reversed: Righteousness Given
paras: At Romans 3:21 the sky changes: “But now.” Two short words, and the whole letter turns on them. A righteousness from God has been revealed apart from the law — not achieved but given, not earned at the counter but handed over. You are “justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.” God sent Christ “to be an atoning sacrifice, through faith in his blood.” Abraham is Paul’s proof: “Abraham believed God, and it was accounted to him for righteousness.”

Sit with the strangeness of it. God “justifies the ungodly” (Romans 4:5) — not the improved, not the trending upward, but the ungodly. Justification is not God noticing that you finally cleaned up. It is God, in Christ, crediting you with a righteousness that was never yours. The dust does not turn to marble first and then get accepted. The dust is accepted in Christ, and that is the only ground real change ever grows from.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: The New Standing: Peace and Access
paras: Romans 5 spells out what the verdict brings. “We have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ.” The hostility between you and God is over — not because you surrendered well, but because Christ made peace by His blood. “We also have our access by faith into this grace in which we stand.” The door guilt kept slamming now stands open, and the floor you stand on will not give way.

And the love behind it is proved at your worst: “while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” Not because you were lovely. While you were still the problem. That is why Paul can reason from the greater to the lesser: “much more, being reconciled, we will be saved by his life.” If God made peace with His enemies at the cost of His Son, He will not now let His reconciled son slip.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: Two Men, Two Worlds
paras: Then Paul pulls the camera back and shows you two men who each carry a world. Through Adam’s one trespass, condemnation and death reached everyone downstream. That is the deepest reason you are dust. Through Christ’s one act of righteousness, justification and life reach everyone joined to Him: “For as through the one man’s disobedience many were made sinners, even so through the obedience of the one, many will be made righteous.”

This is the hinge the rest of the letter swings on. You were born into Adam’s ruin without choosing it. In Christ you are given a standing you could never build. Everything in Romans 6–8 — freedom from sin’s reign, the honest struggle with the flesh, the life of the Spirit — unpacks what it means to be in Christ instead of in Adam. So come to this week as you are. You are not here to manage your standing with God. You are here to find out it was settled at a cross.

stations.verse: As it is written, “There is no one righteous; no, not one. There is no one who understands. There is no one who seeks after God. They have all turned away. They have together become unprofitable. There is no one who does good, no, not so much as one.
stations.question: Where do you exempt yourself from this verdict by comparing yourself with men you think are worse?

stations.verse: for all have sinned, and fall short of the glory of God;
stations.question: Where are you respectable and still short of the glory of God?
stations.live: Stop asking whether you are doing enough to be accepted. Start from the verdict — declared righteous in Christ — and live this week out of it, not for it.
body: Dikaioō is a courtroom word, not a hospital word. In the Greek Old Testament it describes a judge’s ruling: judges “shall justify the righteous, and condemn the wicked” (Deuteronomy 25:1). It does not mean God slowly makes you a little more righteous over time. It means God the Judge declares you righteous in a single verdict, on the ground of Christ’s righteousness counted to you. That is why justification can be complete while your character is still under construction. You are not on probation, hoping the verdict holds if you behave. The gavel has come down in your favor, and it is Christ’s record the court is reading.

stations.verse: being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus; whom God sent to be an atoning sacrifice, through faith in his blood, for a demonstration of his righteousness through the passing over of prior sins, in God’s forbearance;
stations.question: If you are justified freely by His grace, what are you still trying to pay for?
stations.gloss: redemption, release by payment of a ransom
stations.live: When you catch yourself acting like you still owe the old master this week, say it plainly: I was bought. Then name the One who paid.
body: Apolytrōsis is built on lytron, a ransom — the price paid to set a captive free. Paul says you are justified “through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.” Your release was not an amnesty or a shrug. It was a purchase, and the price was the blood of the Son of God. The same word returns in Romans 8:23, where it names “the redemption of our body.” What Christ paid for at the cross He will finish at the resurrection. You have been bought out, and nothing about the purchase is partial.

moreStudies.gloss: place of atonement, mercy seat; atoning sacrifice
moreStudies.xref: Romans 3:25; Hebrews 9:5; Exodus 25:17 and Leviticus 16:2 (Greek OT)
body: In the Greek Old Testament, hilastērion names the mercy seat — the gold cover over the ark where blood was sprinkled on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16). Hebrews 9:5 uses it the same way. Paul says God sent Christ “to be an atoning sacrifice, through faith in his blood,” and the word behind “atoning sacrifice” is hilastērion. The cross is where God’s just anger against sin was not waved off but met and satisfied. The old word for it is propitiation: wrath turned away because it has been fully borne. The hostility did not end because God decided sin did not matter. It ended because sin’s weight landed on Christ.
moreStudies.live: When shame says God is still angry with you, go back to the mercy seat. The wrath you fear already fell on Jesus, and there is none left over for a man in Him.

stations.verse: Now to him who works, the reward is not counted as grace, but as something owed. But to him who doesn’t work, but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is accounted for righteousness.
stations.question: Do you believe God justified you as ungodly, or do you think you were a slightly better candidate than most?
stations.live: Name the thing that made you asebēs. Then read Romans 4:5 out loud with that thing in mind, and let the verse stand.
body: Asebēs is built from sebō, “to revere,” with a negative in front: a man without reverence for God. Paul uses it twice in two chapters, and both times the shock is where he puts it. God “justifies the ungodly” (4:5). “At the right time Christ died for the ungodly” (5:6). Not the devout. Not the almost ready. The word leaves no room for you to bring a résumé. The only qualification for the justifying grace of God is the one you were trying to hide.

stations.verse: Being therefore justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ;
stations.question: Is your life with God built on a peace already made, or on a truce you keep renegotiating by your performance?
stations.live: Pray this week like a man who has been let in. Skip the throat-clearing, come straight to the Father through Christ, and say what you need.
body: Prosagōgē comes from prosagō, “to bring to.” It is the word for being brought into a presence you could not enter on your own. Paul says that through Christ “we also have our access by faith into this grace in which we stand.” Guilt keeps a man in the hallway, hat in hand, waiting to be called. Justification puts him in the room. And look at the verb that follows: stand. Not crouch, not hover at the door. The access is not a visitor’s pass that expires when you fail. It is Christ’s own standing, given to you.

stations.verse: For while we were yet weak, at the right time Christ died for the ungodly. For one will hardly die for a righteous man. Yet perhaps for a righteous person someone would even dare to die. But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.
stations.question: Where are you still trying to earn a love God already proved at the cross?

stations.verse: For if while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, being reconciled, we will be saved by his life.
stations.question: Where do you need the “much more” of this verse to steady you this week?

stations.verse: So then as through one trespass, all men were condemned; even so through one act of righteousness, all men were justified to life. For as through the one man’s disobedience many were made sinners, even so through the obedience of the one, many will be made righteous.
stations.question: When temptation or failure comes, which man are you living out of — Adam or Christ?

stations.verse: for by grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God, not of works, that no one would boast.
stations.question: Where would you rather perform for God than receive from Him?

stations.verse: Behold, his soul is puffed up. It is not upright in him, but the righteous will live by his faith.
stations.question: In what one area this week could you live by faith instead of by feeling or scorekeeping?

stations.verse: For we have all become like one who is unclean, and all our righteousness is like a polluted garment. We all fade like a leaf; and our iniquities, like the wind, take us away.
stations.question: Which of your good deeds have you been quietly counting as your standing before God?
pulls: You do not fight your way to peace with God. You live from a peace He already made at the cross.

practices.title: NAME THE VERDICT YOU ACTUALLY LIVE BY
practices.body: You carry a felt verdict that has nothing to do with the cross: God is pleased with me today, or God is tired of me today. It rises and falls with your week. Catch it this week. When it swings, say out loud: “My standing is not today’s scorecard. I have been justified by faith, and I have peace with God through Jesus Christ.”

practices.title: RECEIVE BEFORE YOU ACHIEVE
practices.body: Before you try to change one thing about your behavior, spend the week receiving what is already true. Each morning, before your feet hit the floor, say it plainly: “I am accepted in Christ. The gift is already given.” You are not priming yourself to earn God’s love. You are letting the love that is already yours become the soil everything else grows in.

practices.title: TAKE YOUR LEDGER TO THE SON
practices.body: Write down the failures you have been tallying and the good deeds you hope will count. Bring that page to Jesus by name: “This whole account was settled at Your cross.” Then tear it up. When the old accusation comes back, answer it with one word: justified.

practices.title: ASK THE SPIRIT TO MAKE IT LAND
practices.body: Justification is true whether you feel it or not. The Holy Spirit is the One who presses God’s love into the heart (Romans 5:5). Each morning this week, pray one sentence: “Holy Spirit, make what is true of me in Christ real to me today.” Then watch for the moments the peace holds where it used to slip.

practices.title: SAY IT TO ONE MAN
practices.body: Sin and self-righteousness both grow in the dark. Before the week ends, tell one brother the ground you are learning to stand on — not your performance but the verdict spoken over you in Christ. Ask him to remind you of it on the day you forget.

title: The Dust and the Verdict
subtitle: from wrath to peace with God
keyVerse: Being therefore justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ.

passage.text: Being therefore justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ;
through whom we also have our access by faith into this grace in which we stand. We rejoice in hope of the glory of God.
Not only this, but we also rejoice in our sufferings, knowing that suffering produces perseverance;
and perseverance, proven character; and proven character, hope:
and hope doesn’t disappoint us, because God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who was given to us.
For while we were yet weak, at the right time Christ died for the ungodly.
For one will hardly die for a righteous man. Yet perhaps for a righteous person someone would even dare to die.
But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.
Much more then, being now justified by his blood, we will be saved from God’s wrath through him.
For if while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, being reconciled, we will be saved by his life.
Not only so, but we also rejoice in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received the reconciliation.

stationsIntro: Read each passage slowly, with your Bible open if you can. Let the verse land before you go to the question. Then answer honestly in the lines provided.
lifeIntro: This week is not about mastering Romans or fixing your behavior by Friday. It is about moving the center of your Christian life off your performance and onto Christ’s finished work.
prayer: Father, I come with nothing in my hands. I have sinned, and I fall short of Your glory. Thank You that You justify the ungodly, and that I stand in grace because of Jesus. Lord Jesus, You bore the wrath I earned; You are my peace and my only record. Holy Spirit, pour the love of God into my heart today, and let me live from the verdict, not for it. Amen.
prayerLines: Father, I come with nothing in my hands.
I have sinned, and I fall short of Your glory.
Thank You that You justify the ungodly,
and that I stand in grace because of Jesus.
Lord Jesus, You bore the wrath I earned;
You are my peace and my only record.
Holy Spirit, pour the love of God into my heart today,
and let me live from the verdict, not for it. Amen.
bottomLine: In Christ you have already been declared righteous and brought to peace with God. You are not walking toward a verdict you have to earn. You are walking from one Christ secured at the cross.
benediction: Before this study asks you to change anything, it asks you to look up and see that the hardest part is finished. The dust you are is real, and the diagnosis is true. But it is not the last word spoken over you. At a cross outside Jerusalem, God set forth His Son as the mercy seat, and the wrath your sin deserved fell there instead of on you. The hostility ended. Not with your surrender. With His.

Lift up your eyes when the felt verdict says God is disappointed — the real verdict was read at Calvary, and it said righteous. Lift up your eyes when the ledger of your failures runs long — the account was settled in His blood. Lift up your eyes when you are tempted to stand at the door like a stranger — you have access, and the floor under you will hold.

You do not begin this study as a defendant waiting on the jury. You begin it justified, at peace, and standing in grace. A guilty man clinging to the ground hears a Judge who is also a Father say: not condemned. Romans 6, 7 and 8 are simply learning to walk as the man that verdict has already made you.
closingVerse: You were dust under wrath. In Christ you are a son at peace. Lift up your eyes and walk like it.
carry: Where are you still living as though the verdict over you were unsettled?

sections.heading: Grace Does Not License Sin — It Ends Its Reign
pulls: You do not resist sin to become free. You resist it because an empty grave already freed you.
paras: Last week closed on news that sounds almost reckless: “where sin abounded, grace abounded more exceedingly.” Paul knows what the human heart does with news like that. It looks for the loophole. If grace covers sin, why not keep sinning? His answer is not a lecture on willpower. It is a funeral notice: “We who died to sin, how could we live in it any longer?” You cannot go on living in the place you died to. A Christian does not treat grace as a license, because something happened to him in Christ. He died, and he was raised.

This is the turn from chapter 5 to chapter 6. Justification answered one question: how can a guilty man be accepted? Now Paul answers the next one every honest believer asks: if I am accepted, what breaks sin’s grip on me? His answer is not “try harder.” It is “you already died to it — now count it true.” Freedom does not begin with effort. It begins with a grave.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: United With Him: Buried and Raised
paras: Paul points to baptism as a picture of something real: “all we who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death.” “We were buried therefore with him through baptism into death, that just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we also might walk in newness of life.” This is the doctrine under everything else — union with Christ. When He died, you died. When He was raised, you were raised. Not by imitation, copying His example from a distance, but by union, His history made yours.

Notice that this comes as a fact before it is ever given as a duty. Paul does not say, try to die to sin. He says, you died. The Christian life is not the desperate project of killing an old self that is still alive. It is the daily, Spirit-given outworking of an old self already crucified. That changes the whole posture of the struggle, from anxious striving to glad agreement with a verdict handed down at the tomb.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: The Old Man Crucified
paras: Paul goes deeper than forgiveness: “our old man was crucified with him, that the body of sin might be done away with, so that we would no longer be in bondage to sin.” The cross did not only pay sin’s penalty. It broke sin’s power. Sin held a title deed to you, and that title has been cancelled. A prisoner who is pardoned may still sit in the cell. A prisoner who is pardoned and released walks out the door. You are the second man.

Be honest, though. Sin still speaks. It still knocks, and it still stirs appetites you thought were buried. So be clear about what “dead to sin” means. It does not mean sin is absent. It means sin is dethroned. Its presence lingers in the dust; its reign is over. That is why the command in verse 11 reads, “consider yourselves also to be dead to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus our Lord.” Not pretend. Count it true, because God has said it is.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: Reign, Not Residence
paras: What do you do with a dethroned tenant who still lives in the house? Paul tells you: “don’t let sin reign in your mortal body.” “Do not present your members to sin as instruments of unrighteousness, but present yourselves to God as alive from the dead.” Sin may still live in your body for now. It may not rule it.

The daily work comes down to one repeated act: handing yourself over, member by member and hour by hour, to God and not to the old master. Your eyes, your hands, your tongue, your imagination — each goes to one owner or the other, all day long. That is not a grim program. It is the ordinary life of a man who has been raised and is learning to use his hands for the One who raised him.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: Not Under Law, but Under Grace
paras: The promise attached to the command is why the command does not crush: “sin will not have dominion over you. For you are not under law, but under grace.” Grace is not the reason sin gets to stay in charge. Grace is the power that puts it out. Under law, sin condemned you and used the law’s demands against you. Under grace, you belong to Another, and He does not let go of what He bought.

So the order holds. First the fact: you died with Christ and were raised with Him. Then the counting: consider it true. Then the presenting: hand your members to God. The dust-man does not dust himself off here either. He is raised with Christ, and then he learns, one ordinary hour at a time, to walk like a man who has been raised.

stations.verse: May it never be! We who died to sin, how could we live in it any longer?
stations.question: Where have you treated grace as permission to keep a sin comfortable?

stations.verse: We were buried therefore with him through baptism into death, that just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we also might walk in newness of life.
stations.question: In what one area are you living in old-grave habits when newness of life is open to you right now?
stations.live: When an old pattern calls you by your old name this week, answer it: “That was buried with Christ. I do not live there anymore.”
body: Synthaptō joins syn, “together with,” to the verb for burial. Paul does not say your old life was paused or put on probation. He says it was buried, and buried with Christ. Burial is how every people on earth says something is finished; nobody buries the living. The old self, the man you were in Adam, was carried to the grave in the death of Jesus. That is why your struggle against sin is never an effort to become a new man by grit. It is learning to live as the man the tomb already released.

Symphytos comes from a verb meaning “to make to grow together.” It is a gardener’s word more than a lawyer’s, and it appears only here in the New Testament. Paul says “we have become united with him in the likeness of his death.” Your union with Christ is not a label stuck on the outside. It is closer to a graft — two lives grown into one, so that what happens to the root happens to the branch. Because you are joined to Him in His death, Paul says with the same confidence, “we will also be part of his resurrection.”
moreStudies.live: Picture a graft bound tight on a young tree. When you feel far from Christ this week, remember that the union does not rest on the feeling. Pray from inside it.

stations.verse: knowing this, that our old man was crucified with him, that the body of sin might be done away with, so that we would no longer be in bondage to sin.
stations.question: Do you treat sin as an unbeaten master you are afraid of, or as a crucified one you are called to stop obeying?
stations.gloss: the old man, the old self
stations.live: Stop introducing yourself to your sin as its servant. The old man was crucified. Live as the new one Christ raised.
body: The palaios anthrōpos — the “old man,” as the World English Bible keeps it — is not your body, your personality or your temperament. It is the whole man you were in Adam, ruled by sin and turned away from God. Paul’s claim is that this old man “was crucified with him”: a finished event, not a project you are still trying to complete. The sin you still feel is not the old man back from the dead. It is the pull of a regime that has already been executed. You are not two men in a fair contest. You are a new man learning to stop taking orders from the old one.

moreStudies.gloss: to make idle, render powerless, do away with
body: Katargeō is built on argos, “idle, out of work.” To katargeō something is to put it out of work. The World English Bible renders Romans 6:6 “that the body of sin might be done away with.” The word does not promise that sinful desire vanishes overnight. It says sin’s ruling power has been put out of commission. Picture a crew boss fired from the job who still hangs around the gate shouting orders. He is loud, and he can still do damage if you listen. But he no longer runs the work. Paul uses the same verb in 7:6 — “we have been discharged from the law” — and 2 Timothy 1:10 uses it for what Christ did to death itself.
moreStudies.live: Name the sin that shouts loudest. A fired boss only runs the men who keep taking his orders. Stop reporting for work.

stations.verse: For he who has died has been freed from sin.
stations.question: Where are you waiting to feel free before you will act free?

stations.verse: Thus consider yourselves also to be dead to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus our Lord.
stations.question: What would counting yourself dead to sin and alive to God change about tomorrow morning?

stations.verse: Therefore don’t let sin reign in your mortal body, that you should obey it in its lusts. Also, do not present your members to sin as instruments of unrighteousness, but present yourselves to God as alive from the dead, and your members as instruments of righteousness to God.
stations.question: Which member — eyes, hands, tongue, imagination — do you most often present to sin?

stations.verse: For sin will not have dominion over you. For you are not under law, but under grace.
stations.question: Where have you been using grace as an excuse instead of leaning on it as strength?
stations.gloss: to be lord over, to have dominion
stations.live: In the moment of temptation this week, ask the question out loud: “Who is lord here?” Then answer it with your next step.
body: Kyrieuō is built from kyrios, “lord.” Paul uses it three times in these chapters. Death “no longer has dominion” over the risen Christ (6:9). Sin “will not have dominion over you” (6:14). The law “has dominion over a man for as long as he lives” (7:1). The question was never whether you would live under a lord, but which one. Sin can still harass you and tempt you. What it cannot do is sit on the throne, because the Lord who holds the deed to you has already risen out of death’s dominion and taken you with Him.

stations.verse: I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.
stations.question: When you sin, whose life are you trying to protect or please?

stations.verse: If then you were raised together with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated on the right hand of God. Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth. For you died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.
stations.question: Where are you living as if your life were exposed and up for grabs instead of hidden with Christ in God?

stations.verse: Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new.
stations.question: What old label do you need to stop wearing this week?

stations.verse: He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree, that we, having died to sins, might live to righteousness. You were healed by his wounds.
stations.question: Have you taken the forgiveness of the cross and left the freedom on the table?

stations.verse: I will also give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you. I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh. I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes. You will keep my ordinances and do them.
stations.question: Where are you trying to power your obedience from your own resources instead of the Spirit God put within you?
pulls: Sin still lives in the house. But it no longer holds the deed. The empty grave took the keys.

practices.title: COUNT IT BEFORE YOU FEEL IT
practices.body: In Romans 6 faith is spelled consider: count it true because God said it, not because you feel it yet. When sin tells you it still owns you, answer with the fact: “I died to that in Christ, and I am alive to God.” You are not lying to yourself. You are agreeing with God. Feeling follows counting far more often than it leads.

practices.title: NAME ONE FIRED BOSS
practices.body: The flesh will try to overwhelm you with the whole list. Refuse it. Pick one sin that has been acting like your lord and treat it all week as the dethroned thing it is. Do not merely resist it; renounce its claim: “You are not lord here. I don’t take your orders.”

practices.title: BRING THE OLD MAN TO THE CROSS
practices.body: You will be tempted to protect and please a self that was already crucified. Take that self — the image, the appetite, the reflex — to Jesus by name: “This was crucified with You. Live Your life in me here.” When the old craving returns, go back to the cross before you argue with it.

practices.title: PRESENT YOUR MEMBERS EACH MORNING
practices.body: Before you reach for your phone, hand over the members the flesh usually grabs: “Father, my eyes are Yours today, and my hands, my tongue and my imagination. I present them to You as instruments of righteousness.” Then watch for the mid-morning moment one of them gets contested, and present it again on the spot.

practices.title: WALK IT OUT WITH A BROTHER
practices.body: Nobody walks out of an old habit alone, and sin loves the dark. Before the week ends, tell one trusted man the sin you named and the member you are presenting to God. Ask him to check on you within ten days.

title: Dead to Sin, Alive to God
subtitle: from dust to the empty grave
keyVerse: Thus consider yourselves also to be dead to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus our Lord.

passage.text: What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound?
May it never be! We who died to sin, how could we live in it any longer?
Or don’t you know that all we who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death?
We were buried therefore with him through baptism into death, that just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we also might walk in newness of life.
For if we have become united with him in the likeness of his death, we will also be part of his resurrection;
knowing this, that our old man was crucified with him, that the body of sin might be done away with, so that we would no longer be in bondage to sin.
For he who has died has been freed from sin.
But if we died with Christ, we believe that we will also live with him;
knowing that Christ, being raised from the dead, dies no more. Death no longer has dominion over him!
For the death that he died, he died to sin one time; but the life that he lives, he lives to God.
Thus consider yourselves also to be dead to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus our Lord.
Therefore don’t let sin reign in your mortal body, that you should obey it in its lusts.
Also, do not present your members to sin as instruments of unrighteousness, but present yourselves to God as alive from the dead, and your members as instruments of righteousness to God.
For sin will not have dominion over you. For you are not under law, but under grace.

stationsLabel: THE WORD ON FREEDOM IN CHRIST
stationsIntro: Read each passage slowly. Let it tell you what is already true of you in Christ before it asks anything of you. Then answer honestly in the lines provided.
lifeIntro: This week is not about white-knuckling your way out of a sin by Friday. It is about counting on a death and resurrection that already happened to you in Christ, and presenting yourself to God member by member.
prayer: Father, I was buried with Christ and raised with Him. Sin still stirs in me, but it does not rule me. Lord Jesus, my old man was crucified with You; I will not take orders from a dead master today. I present my eyes, my hands and my tongue to God. Holy Spirit, make the empty tomb real in me, and walk me in newness of life from this morning until I lie down tonight. Amen.
prayerLines: Father, I was buried with Christ and raised with Him.
Sin still stirs in me, but it does not rule me.
Lord Jesus, my old man was crucified with You;
I will not take orders from a dead master today.
I present my eyes, my hands and my tongue to God.
Holy Spirit, make the empty tomb real in me,
and walk me in newness of life
from this morning until I lie down tonight. Amen.
bottomLine: You do not become free by trying hard enough. Christ has already made you free. Sin’s penalty was paid, its power was broken and its reign was ended in the death and resurrection you share with Him. Count it true, present yourself to God, and take the next step out of the grave.
benediction: Before you ever swung at the sin that keeps winning, it was disarmed at a cross and left behind in a tomb. The flesh will drag your gaze down to the relapse and the craving that will not seem to die, and it will tell you nothing has changed. It is lying. You were joined to Jesus in His death, and the old man sin used to own was nailed up with Him and buried.

Lift up your eyes when the old appetite acts like it still owns the house — the deed changed hands at Calvary. Lift up your eyes when you stumble an hour after resolving not to — a dethroned king can still shout, but he cannot reign over a man who belongs to Christ. Lift up your eyes when morning comes and the struggle feels the same — Christ was raised “through the glory of the Father,” and that same glory stands behind your newness of life.

You are not straining toward a freedom you hope to earn. You are standing in one the empty grave already bought, learning step by step to live like it is true. Death “no longer has dominion” over your risen Lord. It has none over the man hidden with Him in God.
closingVerse: The power that emptied the tomb broke sin’s crown over you. Count it true, and walk out.
carry: Where are you still serving a master Christ has already dethroned?

sections.heading: Everyone Serves Someone
pulls: Freedom is not having no master. It is finally belonging to the One whose service is life.
paras: For the second time in this chapter Paul raises the loophole — “Shall we sin, because we are not under law, but under grace?” — and for the second time he answers, “May it never be!” This time he reaches for a different picture. Last week it was death and resurrection. This week it is a master’s household. The point that governs everything is simple: you were never offered the option of having no master. The Good News does not set you loose to be your own god. It moves you from one ownership to another, out from under a master who pays in death and into the service of a Master who gives life.

That matters for how you think about freedom. You picture freedom as no lord, no yoke, no one to answer to. Scripture calls that the oldest bondage there is: a man serving himself and calling it liberty. Real freedom is not the absence of a master. It is finally belonging to the right one — the One whose yoke is easy, whose burden is light, and whose gift is eternal life.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: The Master You Obey
paras: Paul’s logic in verse 16 is hard to escape: “when you present yourselves as servants and obey someone, you are the servants of whomever you obey; whether of sin to death, or of obedience to righteousness.” You become the servant of whatever you keep obeying. There is no third door marked neutral. Every yielding is a quiet declaration of who owns you.

You do not usually choose a master by signing a contract. You choose one a thousand small yieldings at a time: the second look, the sharp reply, the private indulgence. Each is a quiet “yes, sir” to a master Christ already threw out. Grace does not make those yieldings harmless. It makes them absurd — a freed man walking back to a cell whose door is standing open.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: The Change of Ownership
paras: Then Paul breaks into thanks: “But thanks be to God, that, whereas you were bondservants of sin, you became obedient from the heart to that form of teaching to which you were delivered. Being made free from sin, you became bondservants of righteousness.” Look at the tense. It is done. You were a bondservant of sin. You have been made free. You have become a bondservant of righteousness. This is not a promotion you are working toward. It is a change of ownership already recorded in heaven.

And look where the new obedience comes from: “from the heart.” This is not a slave gritting his teeth under a new overseer. It is a changed heart that wants a new Master. The heart of stone has been replaced, as Ezekiel promised, and it beats toward God.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: Freedom Has a Direction
paras: Paul is plain about how it works out: “as you presented your members as servants to uncleanness and to wickedness upon wickedness, even so now present your members as servants to righteousness for sanctification.” The same members you once handed to impurity — eyes, hands, tongue — are now handed, on purpose and daily, to righteousness.

Service to sin ran downhill, wickedness upon wickedness. Service to God runs toward sanctification, one yielding building on the next until the whole life is being remade. Freedom is not standing still in an empty field. It is walking somewhere, with Someone, toward holiness.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: Two Harvests
paras: Then Paul makes you look down the road. “What fruit then did you have at that time in the things of which you are now ashamed? For the end of those things is death.” The old master always looked generous up front and left you ashamed and empty-handed at the end. “But now, being made free from sin and having become servants of God, you have your fruit of sanctification and the result of eternal life.” Two masters. Two harvests. Two ends.

The passage lands on its best-known verse: “For the wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.” Sin pays wages. You earn them, you are owed them, and the currency is death. God does not pay wages at all. He gives a free gift, and the gift is life. If God dealt with you in wages, you would be paid in full, and paid in death. The dust-man does not get what he earned. In Christ he gets what Christ earned.

stations.verse: Don’t you know that when you present yourselves as servants and obey someone, you are the servants of whomever you obey; whether of sin to death, or of obedience to righteousness?
stations.question: Whom have your recent yieldings actually been serving?

stations.verse: But thanks be to God, that, whereas you were bondservants of sin, you became obedient from the heart to that form of teaching to which you were delivered. Being made free from sin, you became bondservants of righteousness.
stations.question: Where are you serving God like a resentful hired hand instead of a freed and willing servant?
stations.live: Stop asking what you want to do with your life as if you owned it. Ask what your Master, who loves you, wants — and find that freer than running your own life ever was.
body: Doulos is a stronger word than “servant” wants to be. A hired man can quit. A doulos is owned. The World English Bible renders it “bondservant,” and Paul uses it on purpose for the Christian: you have not been made your own; you have been bought, and you belong to God. He uses it of himself in the first line of the letter — “Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ” (1:1). That sounds like bad news in a culture that prizes owning yourself, until you see who the Master is. To be the doulos of a cruel master is misery. To be the doulos of the God who gave His Son for you is the truest freedom a man can know.

stations.verse: I speak in human terms because of the weakness of your flesh, for as you presented your members as servants to uncleanness and to wickedness upon wickedness, even so now present your members as servants to righteousness for sanctification.
stations.question: Which direction is your present pattern running — toward more wickedness or toward sanctification?
stations.live: When temptation dresses sin up as freedom and obedience as bondage this week, call it what it is. The open door leads toward God, not back to the cell.
body: Eleutheroō is the word for setting someone free. Paul uses it in the past tense: “being made free from sin” (6:18), “being made free from sin and having become servants of God” (6:22). This is not freedom you are negotiating toward. It was granted at the cross. And notice what the freedom is for. You were not freed into a vacuum of self-rule; that is only the old bondage in new clothes. You were freed into the service of God, where obedience is not a cage but the shape your liberty takes.

stations.verse: For when you were servants of sin, you were free from righteousness. What fruit then did you have at that time in the things of which you are now ashamed? For the end of those things is death.
stations.question: What did the old master actually pay you?

stations.verse: But now, being made free from sin and having become servants of God, you have your fruit of sanctification and the result of eternal life.
stations.question: Where do you still expect God’s way to leave you empty?
stations.live: When you fear you are about to get what you deserve, remember the ledger. Your wage was death, and Jesus took it. What is left for you is gift.
body: Opsōnion was the pay handed to a soldier — his provisions and his wage. Luke 3:14 uses it that way. It is what a man has earned and is owed. Paul’s point is sharp: sin keeps its books. It always pays, and the wage it owes is death. Set against that, Paul does not say that the wages of God is life. That would ruin the Good News. He changes words: the free gift. God does not run a payroll. If He did, every man would collect exactly what he earned. Instead Christ took the wage you had coming, at the cross.

stations.verse: For the wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.
stations.question: What are you still trying to earn that God only ever gives?
stations.gloss: free gift, a gift of grace
stations.live: Name one thing you have been straining to deserve from God. Then receive it as charisma — already given, in Christ, for nothing.
body: Charisma comes from charis, “grace.” It is a gift defined by the generosity of the giver, not the worth of the one who receives it. Paul uses it in chapter 5 — “But the free gift isn’t like the trespass” (5:15) — and brings it back at the end of chapter 6 to set against opsōnion. On one side, wages earned and paid in death. On the other, a gift of grace you did nothing to deserve, received as life. That is why a Christian can neither boast nor despair. Both put the weight back on his performance. The charisma puts it on Christ.

stations.verse: Jesus answered them, “Most certainly I tell you, everyone who commits sin is the bondservant of sin. A bondservant doesn’t live in the house forever. A son remains forever. If therefore the Son makes you free, you will be free indeed.
stations.question: Where are you chasing a self-made freedom that is really another bondage?

stations.verse: Stand firm therefore in the liberty by which Christ has made us free, and don’t be entangled again with a yoke of bondage.
stations.question: What old yoke are you in danger of taking up again?

stations.verse: For you, brothers, were called for freedom. Only don’t use your freedom for gain to the flesh, but through love be servants to one another.
stations.question: Where might you be using your freedom in Christ as cover for the flesh?

stations.verse: who gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity, and purify for himself a people for his own possession, zealous for good works.
stations.question: Do you live as a man glad to be owned by Christ, or as one who still thinks he belongs to himself?
stations.live: Stop believing God’s ways are the narrow place. Step into one of His commands this week the way you would step out into open country.
body: The psalmist says, “I will walk in liberty, for I have sought your precepts” (Psalm 119:45). The Hebrew behind “in liberty” is formed from rāḥāḇ, “broad, wide”: literally, to walk in a wide place. It is the same word God used for the land He promised Israel, “a good and large land” (Exodus 3:8). The psalmist pictures freedom as open country with room to move. And look at what gives it to him: God’s precepts. The world calls God’s commands the narrow cell and self-rule the open field. The psalm turns it around. Sin is the cramped place that keeps shrinking. God’s way is open ground.

stations.verse: For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus made me free from the law of sin and of death.
stations.question: Where do you need to lean on the Spirit’s power instead of your willpower?
pulls: The old master pays in full, and he pays in death. Your new Master took that wage Himself and hands you life for free.

practices.title: ASK WHOM YOU ARE SERVING
practices.body: When a temptation or a decision comes this week, do not only ask whether it is allowed. Ask out loud whom it would serve. Every yielding is an allegiance. Naming the master before you act takes much of sin’s power away, because it can no longer pass itself off as freedom.

practices.title: REFUSE THE WAGE, RECEIVE THE GIFT
practices.body: Catch yourself when you slip into earning mode with God — trying to deserve His favor, or bracing for the wage you think is coming. Each time, say Romans 6:23 back to yourself and add one line: “Christ took my wage. What is left is gift.” Live this week as a man receiving, not an employee on review.

practices.title: BRING YOUR SELF-OWNERSHIP TO THE SON
practices.body: The deepest bondage is the quiet conviction that you belong to yourself. Take that to Jesus by name: “You bought me. I am not my own. I stop running my own kingdom.” Being owned by the One who gave Himself for you is not loss. It is the widest freedom you will ever have.

practices.title: PRESENT ONE MEMBER DAILY
practices.body: Freedom is walked out member by member. Each morning hand the Spirit the one the old master reaches for first — your eyes, your tongue, your time. Then watch for the moment it gets contested, and present it again. Service to sin ran downhill; this small daily yielding runs toward sanctification.

practices.title: WALK IN THE OPEN WITH A BROTHER
practices.body: Freedom is meant to be lived in the open and in company. Before the week ends, tell one trusted man the master you are walking away from and the member you are presenting to God. Ask him to check in. Sin grows in cramped, secret places. Grace grows in open ones.

title: No Longer in Bondage
subtitle: from dust to freedom
keyVerse: But now, being made free from sin and having become servants of God, you have your fruit of sanctification and the result of eternal life.

passage.text: What then? Shall we sin, because we are not under law, but under grace? May it never be!
Don’t you know that when you present yourselves as servants and obey someone, you are the servants of whomever you obey; whether of sin to death, or of obedience to righteousness?
But thanks be to God, that, whereas you were bondservants of sin, you became obedient from the heart to that form of teaching to which you were delivered.
Being made free from sin, you became bondservants of righteousness.

I speak in human terms because of the weakness of your flesh, for as you presented your members as servants to uncleanness and to wickedness upon wickedness, even so now present your members as servants to righteousness for sanctification.
For when you were servants of sin, you were free from righteousness.
What fruit then did you have at that time in the things of which you are now ashamed? For the end of those things is death.
But now, being made free from sin and having become servants of God, you have your fruit of sanctification and the result of eternal life.
For the wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.

stationsIntro: Read each passage slowly. Ask not only what you are doing but whom you are serving. Then answer honestly in the lines provided.
lifeIntro: This week is not about feeling free while you keep serving the old master. It is about living as a man who has changed owners: refusing sin’s wages, receiving God’s gift and presenting your members to the Master who gives life.
prayer: Father, I was a bondservant of sin, and You made me free. I belong to You now, and I am glad of it. Lord Jesus, You bought me with Your own blood; You took the wage I had earned. I refuse the old master’s pay today. Holy Spirit, walk me in liberty, and present my members to God through me, one hour and one choice at a time. Amen.
prayerLines: Father, I was a bondservant of sin, and You made me free.
I belong to You now, and I am glad of it.
Lord Jesus, You bought me with Your own blood;
You took the wage I had earned.
I refuse the old master’s pay today.
Holy Spirit, walk me in liberty,
and present my members to God through me,
one hour and one choice at a time. Amen.
bottomLine: You were never offered a life with no master — only a choice of which one. Grace did not make you your own. It bought you, freed you from sin, and gave you to a Master whose service is life and whose gift is eternal. Refuse the old wage, receive the free gift, and present yourself to the God who owns you and loves you.
benediction: Before you look at your chains or your freedom, look at Christ, because the whole story of your release is the story of what He did. The eternal Son, who owed no one anything, “emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:7). He was sold for thirty pieces of silver, bound in a garden at night and led away without a word in His own defense. The free Master walked into the servant’s place so that servants like you could walk out.

Lift up your eyes when the old master calls and dresses himself up as liberty — the One who was bound so you could be loosed is calling louder. Lift up your eyes when old habit walks you back toward the cell — the wage was paid in full, and the deed to your life is in nail-scarred hands. Lift up your eyes when obedience feels like a cage — your Master is the Shepherd who lays down His life for the sheep, and His service is open country.

You are not obeying to buy a freedom you lack. You are living out a freedom Jesus bought with His own blood. Every step away from sin is not a payment toward liberty. It is a glad walk toward the Master who loved you and gave Himself for you.
closingVerse: The door is open, the wage is paid, and the Master is calling. Lift up your eyes and walk in liberty.
carry: Whose voice are you still obeying as though you owed it something?

sections.heading: Released to Belong
pulls: You were not released from the law to live alone. You were released to belong to Christ and bear His fruit.
paras: Chapter 6 freed you from sin’s reign. Chapter 7 opens by releasing you from something you may not have known was holding you: the law — not as God’s good instruction, but as a covenant of demand that could accuse you and never make you fruitful. Paul reaches for the most intimate picture in human life to explain it. Not a master’s household this time, but a marriage. You have been discharged from an old union that only bore fruit to death, “that you would be joined to another, to him who was raised from the dead, that we might produce fruit to God.”

A man can relate to God, deep down, as a list of rules he keeps failing — a stern first husband whose expectations can never be met, always disappointed, always keeping score. Paul says that marriage is over. You died to it through the body of Christ. You are no longer answering to a contract. You are joined to a risen Christ who loved you enough to die for you, and the whole nature of your life with God has changed from demand to devotion.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: Bound Until Death
paras: Paul builds on a legal principle everyone in his day understood: “the law has dominion over a man for as long as he lives.” He illustrates it with marriage. “For the woman that has a husband is bound by law to the husband while he lives, but if the husband dies, she is discharged from the law of the husband.” Death dissolves the claim. This is not a teaching on divorce. It is an analogy with one point: a binding covenant is ended by death, and once it is ended, a new belonging is not betrayal but freedom.

Watch what Paul does with who dies. In the picture, the husband dies and the wife is freed. In the application, it is not the law that dies. It is you: “you also were made dead to the law through the body of Christ.” That is better news than it sounds. A law that simply died could no longer show you God’s will. But a man who has died to the law’s claim is released from it while the law itself stays holy. The claim is dissolved not by lowering God’s standard, but by your death with Christ.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: Joined to the Risen Christ
paras: Every phrase of verse 4 carries weight. “You also were made dead to the law” — the old covenant of works no longer holds you. “Through the body of Christ” — the death happened in His crucified body, the same union you studied in chapter 6. “That you would be joined to another” — the purpose was never mere release; it was a new union. And the other is not a set of demands but a risen Person: “him who was raised from the dead.”

Why the new union? “That we might produce fruit to God.” The old one could not. A man can live his whole life married to the rules — effort, resolutions, guilt — and never bear one lasting fruit, because law can command fruit but cannot grow it. Only union with the living Christ produces the real thing. That is why trying harder never works, and why belonging to Christ always, in time, bears.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: Two Kinds of Fruit
paras: Paul names what each union produced. “For when we were in the flesh, the sinful passions which were through the law worked in our members to bring out fruit to death.” Under the old arrangement the law actually stirred up what it forbade. You will feel the full weight of that next week. The fruit of that marriage was death, every time.

The new union bears a different harvest. It is not the product of a stricter marriage to the rules. It is the fruit of a living union with the risen Lord. A branch does not strain to produce grapes. It stays in the vine.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: Newness of the Spirit
paras: Verse 6 sets the whole difference in one sentence: “But now we have been discharged from the law, having died to that in which we were held; so that we serve in newness of the spirit, and not in oldness of the letter.” The oldness of the letter is outside command pressing on a heart that does not want to obey. It produces either pride or despair. The newness of the Spirit is the living God at work inside, growing an obedience that comes from love.

Same God. Same holy standard. An entirely different way of relating to it. The dust-man is not called to try the old marriage harder. He is called to live as one joined to Christ, serving in the newness of the Spirit, and to let the fruit grow the way fruit always grows — out of a living union, not a legal one.

stations.verse: Or don’t you know, brothers (for I speak to men who know the law), that the law has dominion over a man for as long as he lives?
stations.question: Where are you still living as if the law’s old claim of demand and failure were binding on you?

stations.verse: For the woman that has a husband is bound by law to the husband while he lives, but if the husband dies, she is discharged from the law of the husband. So then if, while the husband lives, she is joined to another man, she would be called an adulteress. But if the husband dies, she is free from the law, so that she is no adulteress, though she is joined to another man.
stations.question: Do you ever feel guilty for resting in grace instead of striving under rules?

stations.verse: Therefore, my brothers, you also were made dead to the law through the body of Christ, that you would be joined to another, to him who was raised from the dead, that we might produce fruit to God.
stations.question: Are you living as one joined to a risen Christ, or as the failed partner of a rulebook?
stations.live: Stop straining to manufacture one fruit this week — patience, purity, kindness. Tend the union instead, with time in the Word and prayer each day, and let the fruit be borne.
body: Karpophoreō joins karpos, “fruit,” to pherō, “to bear.” Paul uses it of both unions: the old one worked “to bring out fruit to death” (7:5); the new one exists “that we might produce fruit to God” (7:4). The word is organic on purpose. A branch does not manufacture fruit by effort. It bears fruit out of its union with the vine. That is the quiet end of legalism: you cannot produce the fruit of a Christlike life by trying harder at the rules. It is borne by belonging to the risen Christ.

stations.verse: For when we were in the flesh, the sinful passions which were through the law worked in our members to bring out fruit to death.
stations.question: Where has white-knuckled rule-keeping only made a temptation louder?

stations.verse: But now we have been discharged from the law, having died to that in which we were held; so that we serve in newness of the spirit, and not in oldness of the letter.
stations.question: What one area of your life would change if you moved it from the oldness of the letter to the newness of the Spirit?
stations.gloss: to hold fast, to hold down, to restrain
stations.live: Name what still feels like a grip on you — an old failure, a standard you never met. Say out loud, “I died to that in which I was held,” and walk as a released man.
body: Katechō means to hold fast or hold down. Paul uses it for what the law did under the old arrangement: “having died to that in which we were held.” The law held you the way a creditor holds a debtor — a firm grip, a claim that did not let go. Romans 1:18 uses the same verb for men “who suppress the truth in unrighteousness”: they hold it down. Under the old covenant you were the one held down. In Christ the grip is broken, not because the law was wrong, but because the man it held has died with Christ.

moreStudies.gloss: letter, something written; the written code
body: Gramma is a written letter — the law as written command standing outside the heart. Paul sets it against the Spirit: “we serve in newness of the spirit, and not in oldness of the letter.” The letter could tell you what to do. It could never give you the desire or the power to do it, so it produced either pride or despair. In 2 Corinthians 3:6 Paul says it plainly: “For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.” The difference is not a different God or a lower standard. It is the difference between a rule taped to the wall and a Person living in the house.
moreStudies.live: Where you have been serving by sheer outside effort, ask the Spirit to work from within: “Grow this in me. I cannot tape it on from the outside.”

stations.verse: For I, through the law, died to the law, that I might live to God.
stations.question: Where has clinging to rule-keeping kept you from a living relationship with God?
stations.live: Pick one duty that has gone stale — prayer, church, your marriage. Ask God for newness of the spirit in it this week, and do it expecting Him to meet you there.
body: Kainotēs means newness or freshness, and it appears only twice in the New Testament, both in these chapters. You “walk in newness of life” (6:4), and you “serve in newness of the spirit” (7:6). The two belong together. The life is new because you were raised with Christ. The service is new because the Spirit, not the letter, is at work in it. The Christian life is not your old life with a coat of religious paint. It is a new life, lived in a new way, for a new Master.

stations.verse: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us. For it is written, “Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree,
stations.question: What condemnation are you still living under that Christ already carried?

stations.verse: For I am jealous over you with a godly jealousy. For I married you to one husband, that I might present you as a pure virgin to Christ.
stations.question: Is Christ to you a Bridegroom to be devoted to, or a boss to be satisfied?

stations.verse: Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the assembly, and gave himself up for it; that he might sanctify it, having cleansed it by the washing of water with the word, that he might present the assembly to himself gloriously, not having spot or wrinkle or any such thing; but that it should be holy and without defect.
stations.question: How should being loved like this change the way you obey Him?

stations.verse: wiping out the handwriting in ordinances which was against us. He has taken it out of the way, nailing it to the cross.
stations.question: What old record of debt are you still reading to yourself?

stations.verse: For your Maker is your husband; Yahweh of Armies is his name. The Holy One of Israel is your Redeemer. He will be called the God of the whole earth.
stations.question: Where do you need to trade a distant, contractual view of God for the nearness this verse describes?
stations.gloss: to marry, to be a husband; to be lord over
stations.live: When God feels distant or contractual this week, read Isaiah 54:5 out loud. You belong to His people, and He calls Himself their husband.
body: Bāʿal is the Hebrew verb for being a husband, and it carries the sense of lordship too: in Israel a wife belonged to her husband’s house. Isaiah 54:5 uses it of God Himself: “For your Maker is your husband; Yahweh of Armies is his name.” Jeremiah 31:32 uses it of the old covenant Israel broke, “although I was a husband to them.” Romans 7 announces the new covenant the prophets promised — a union in which God’s people are joined to Him not by a contract they keep failing, but by a Husband who keeps it for both.
pulls: You cannot bear the fruit of a living union by trying harder at an old contract. Belong to Christ, and the fruit is borne.

practices.title: NAME THE OLD CONTRACT
practices.body: You may still relate to God as a disappointed first husband: rules, scorekeeping, never enough. Catch that voice this week and answer it: “That contract is over. I died to the law through the body of Christ.” Say it until the reflex begins to change.

practices.title: TEND THE UNION, NOT THE OUTPUT
practices.body: Pick the one area where you have been straining to produce fruit by effort. This week, stop manufacturing and start abiding. Bring it to Christ in the Word and prayer each day, and ask Him to bear the fruit through the union.

practices.title: OBEY AS ONE WHO IS LOVED
practices.body: Before you obey Christ in some hard thing this week, remember who is asking: the One who “loved the assembly, and gave himself up for it” (Ephesians 5:25). The same command obeyed out of love instead of fear is a different act.

practices.title: ASK THE SPIRIT TO WRITE IT INSIDE
practices.body: Where you have been taping God’s commands to the outside of a reluctant heart, ask the Spirit to write them inside: “I cannot obey this from the outside in. Grow the desire in me.” Then watch for Him to make you want what you once had to force.

practices.title: LET A BROTHER REMIND YOU WHOSE YOU ARE
practices.body: The old contract voice is loudest when you are alone. Tell one trusted man about the shift you are making, from rulebook to relationship, and ask him to remind you, when you slide back into striving, that you belong to Christ.

title: Joined to Another
subtitle: from dust to the new union
keyVerse: Therefore, my brothers, you also were made dead to the law through the body of Christ, that you would be joined to another, to him who was raised from the dead, that we might produce fruit to God.

passage.text: Or don’t you know, brothers (for I speak to men who know the law), that the law has dominion over a man for as long as he lives?
For the woman that has a husband is bound by law to the husband while he lives, but if the husband dies, she is discharged from the law of the husband.

So then if, while the husband lives, she is joined to another man, she would be called an adulteress. But if the husband dies, she is free from the law, so that she is no adulteress, though she is joined to another man.
Therefore, my brothers, you also were made dead to the law through the body of Christ, that you would be joined to another, to him who was raised from the dead, that we might produce fruit to God.
For when we were in the flesh, the sinful passions which were through the law worked in our members to bring out fruit to death.
But now we have been discharged from the law, having died to that in which we were held; so that we serve in newness of the spirit, and not in oldness of the letter.

stationsLabel: THE WORD ON BELONGING TO CHRIST
stationsIntro: Read each passage slowly. Let it move you from relating to God as a rule-keeper to relating to Him as one joined to Christ. Then answer honestly in the lines provided.
lifeIntro: This week is not about finding the willpower to keep the rules better. It is about relating to God in a new way — joined to the risen Christ, released from the old contract, bearing fruit out of union rather than effort.
prayer: Father, I died to the old contract through the body of Christ. I do not come to You today as a failed rule-keeper. Lord Jesus, I am joined to You, risen from the dead; bear Your fruit in me that I cannot produce. Holy Spirit, write God’s law on my heart, and let me serve in newness, not in oldness. Make me want from the inside what You command, and keep me close to Christ all day. Amen.
prayerLines: Father, I died to the old contract through the body of Christ.
I do not come to You today as a failed rule-keeper.
Lord Jesus, I am joined to You, risen from the dead;
bear Your fruit in me that I cannot produce.
Holy Spirit, write God’s law on my heart,
and let me serve in newness, not in oldness.
Make me want from the inside what You command,
and keep me close to Christ all day. Amen.
bottomLine: You have died to the law and been joined to the risen Christ — not to live rule-bound and alone, but to belong to Him and bear fruit to God. The old covenant of demand and failure is discharged. Stop striving under a contract that is over, stay close to the Christ who loves you, and let the Spirit grow what no rulebook could force.
benediction: Let your eyes land on Christ, because everything this week has been about Him. The old arrangement — you and the law, all demand and no power — ended in a death. Look whose death it was. Christ stepped under the law in your place, met every demand you could not meet, and carried its curse to the tree. “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us.” The record against you was nailed to His cross.

Lift up your eyes when the old contract voice hisses, perform or be rejected — the risen Christ has bound His life to yours by a covenant He keeps. Lift up your eyes when you strain for fruit and come up dry — fruit is never squeezed out of a man under law; it grows in a man joined to his Lord. Lift up your eyes when you feel like a hired hand — Christ gave Himself up for His people, to present them to Himself “not having spot or wrinkle or any such thing.”

You do not obey to win His love. You obey because you already have it, bought with His blood and sealed by His resurrection. Stay close to Him. The fruit will come, because it always comes where the vine and the branch are one.
closingVerse: The old contract is buried. You are joined to a risen Christ. Lift up your eyes and love Him back.
carry: Where is Christ inviting you to trade striving for belonging this week?

sections.heading: The Mirror Is Not the Problem
pulls: The law never made you a sinner. It turned on the light and showed you what the dust already was.
paras: Paul has said hard things about the law. You died to it. You were discharged from it. Your sinful passions were even stirred through it. A fair reader starts to wonder whether the law is the villain. Paul recoils: “Is the law sin? May it never be!” Then he spends these verses clearing God’s law of every charge while making the diagnosis of the human heart more honest, not less. The law is like a mirror. It did not put the dirt on your face. It showed you what was already there.

This week matters, because much discouragement comes from blaming the wrong thing. When God’s standard exposes you, the flesh wants to do one of two things: attack the standard (“these rules are unrealistic”) or sink under it (“I will never measure up, so why try”). Paul offers a third way. Let the law do its real work — not to shame you into hiding, and not to be softened into something you can keep, but to diagnose you so honestly that you stop trusting yourself and run to Christ.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: The Light That Exposes
paras: “I wouldn’t have known sin, except through the law. For I wouldn’t have known coveting, unless the law had said, ‘You shall not covet.’” Notice which command Paul picks. Not murder, not theft. The tenth, the one that goes underground into desire. A man can avoid the outward acts and still be full of coveting, and no human court would ever catch him. It takes God’s law to name the sin hiding in the wanting.

That is the mercy inside the law’s severity. A disease you cannot see is a disease you will never treat. The law’s exposure feels like an accusation, and in one sense it is. But it is the accusation of a doctor reading a scan, not a prosecutor building a case for sport. God shows you the sin because He intends to deal with it.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: Sin Finds an Occasion
paras: Then Paul explains a thousand frustrating mornings: “But sin, finding occasion through the commandment, produced in me all kinds of coveting.” Indwelling sin uses the prohibition as a launching point. Tell a fallen heart “do not,” and something in it wakes up and wants to. That is not the law’s fault. The law is good. It is sin’s cunning, turning even a holy command into an occasion for rebellion.

You have felt this. You resolve to stop a habit, and the resolve seems to make the pull stronger. You fence off a sin, and the fence becomes the thing you keep staring at. The problem was never the rule. The problem is a heart bent enough to turn God’s good word into fuel for the flesh. Which means the answer can never be only more rules. A heart like that needs a new life and a Savior.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: Deceived and Killed
paras: Paul names sin’s method: “for sin, finding occasion through the commandment, deceived me, and through it killed me.” And again: “The commandment which was for life, this I found to be for death.” Sin lies. It makes the forbidden look like life and the command look like a cage. Then, having deceived, it kills.

The man who thought he was reaching for freedom finds himself further down in the dust. That is the pattern of every temptation since Eden: a good word from God, a lie about what it withholds, a reach for what looks like life, and death. Seeing the pattern is the first step toward refusing it.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: Holy, Righteous and Good
paras: Then the verdict on the law: “Therefore the law indeed is holy, and the commandment holy, and righteous, and good.” The mirror is clean. Whatever went wrong, it was not God’s standard. Paul presses the diagnosis to its sharpest point: sin was working through what is good “that through the commandment sin might become exceedingly sinful.” The law’s exposing work was designed to unmask sin for the monster it is — not to leave you in despair, but to strip away the illusion that you could manage your way to righteousness.

If the law is holy and the trouble is you, then self-improvement is a dead end and your hope lies outside yourself. That is the honest despair the law is meant to produce, because it is the despair that finally looks up. The mirror can show you the dirt. It cannot wash it off. Only One can, and the whole point of the diagnosis is to send you to Him.

stations.verse: What shall we say then? Is the law sin? May it never be! However, I wouldn’t have known sin, except through the law. For I wouldn’t have known coveting, unless the law had said, “You shall not covet.
stations.question: Where has a command of God exposed something in you that you would rather not have seen?
stations.live: Stop grading yourself on behavior alone this week. Ask where your wanting runs when no one is watching, and bring that ground honestly to God.
body: Ḥāmaḏ is the verb of the tenth commandment: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s house” (Exodus 20:17). It means to desire, to take pleasure in, and in the commandment, to want what is not yours. It is the word Achan uses after he stole from the spoil of Jericho: “then I coveted them and took them” (Joshua 7:21). Desire first, then the hand. That is why Paul reaches for this command in Romans 7. A man can keep his hands clean and his wanting filthy, and the law of God goes all the way down to the wanting.

stations.verse: But sin, finding occasion through the commandment, produced in me all kinds of coveting. For apart from the law, sin is dead.
stations.question: Have you noticed a sin growing stronger the moment you forbade it?
stations.gloss: a starting point; an occasion, opportunity
stations.live: When a prohibition seems to make a temptation louder this week, name what is happening: sin is using the fence as its starting point. Don’t build more fences. Take it to Christ.
body: Aphormē means a starting point. In military writing it named a base of operations, the ground a campaign was launched from. The World English Bible renders it “occasion”: “sin, finding occasion through the commandment.” Sin sets up its operation right at the command. Tell the fallen heart “do not,” and the prohibition becomes the place it launches from. Paul uses the same word in Galatians 5:13: “Only don’t use your freedom for gain to the flesh.” Sin will take any ground you give it — the law’s no or grace’s yes — and try to build on it.

stations.verse: I was alive apart from the law once, but when the commandment came, sin revived, and I died. The commandment which was for life, this I found to be for death;
stations.question: When has trying to find life through rule-keeping left you more condemned?

stations.verse: for sin, finding occasion through the commandment, deceived me, and through it killed me.
stations.question: Where is sin lying to you right now about what will satisfy?
stations.live: Ask what your strongest temptation promises you. Name the lie in one sentence, and set a promise of God beside it.
body: Exapataō is a strengthened form of the ordinary verb for deceiving. Paul says sin “deceived me, and through it killed me.” The same verb appears in 2 Corinthians 11:3: “as the serpent deceived Eve in his craftiness.” Romans 7 is Eden all over again. A good command, a lie about what it withholds, a reach for what looks like life, and death. Sin does not usually come to you looking like death. It comes looking like the thing you have been missing.

stations.verse: Therefore the law indeed is holy, and the commandment holy, and righteous, and good.
stations.question: Where do you quietly blame God’s standard for failures that come from your own heart?

stations.verse: Did then that which is good become death to me? May it never be! But sin, that it might be shown to be sin, was producing death in me through that which is good; that through the commandment sin might become exceedingly sinful.
stations.question: Which sin are you still minimizing that God wants you to see as exceedingly sinful?
stations.gloss: sin; a missing of the mark
stations.live: Stop treating your sin as a habit to be tweaked. Name it as the deadly power it is, and take it to the only One strong enough to break it.
body: Hamartia is the ordinary New Testament word for sin, and at root it means missing the mark. But across these verses Paul describes it almost as a person. It finds occasion, produces, deceives and kills. In 6:12 it wants to “reign”; in 5:12 it “entered into the world.” That matters for an honest diagnosis. Sin is not only the sum of your mistakes, a habit to be adjusted. It is a power at work in you, bent on your death. You will never out-discipline a power like that. It is exactly the kind of enemy only a Savior can beat.

stations.verse: Because by the works of the law, no flesh will be justified in his sight; for through the law comes the knowledge of sin.
stations.question: Where are you still using rule-keeping to earn a standing only Christ can give?

stations.verse: So that the law has become our tutor to bring us to Christ, that we might be justified by faith.
stations.question: Is your failure to meet God’s standard driving you to Christ, or only leaving you in guilt?
stations.live: Receive the command that exposes you this week as a Father’s instruction, not a tyrant’s trap. Read Psalm 19:7–11 once through before you go to bed.
body: Torah means instruction, direction, law — the teaching of a Father showing His children the way. That is why the psalmist can say, “Yahweh’s law is perfect, restoring the soul” (Psalm 19:7). The law that exposes you is also a gift: God telling you the truth about Himself, about goodness and about you. It wounds to heal. To love God’s torah is not legalism. It is treasuring the honest word of a Father who shows you the disease because He means to cure it.
